claims.text: The proposed multiscale method separately computes lattice and electronic thermal transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Separating lattice and electronic transport will produce significantly more accurate conductivity predictions than earlier single-estimate methods.
The modeled HfNbTaTiZr system is a defect-free bulk crystal.
A modeled specimen may contain 1 wt.% oxygen while being treated as the cited experimental system.
An ab initio phonon Boltzmann transport model can quantify the lattice contribution.
DFT-derived electron scattering rates can be used to evaluate the electronic contribution.
Combining the two calculated contributions through a controlled weighting scheme prevents their conflation.
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
High-temperature validation applies over 300–1200 K to specimens containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Local variations in atomic mass and force constants inherent to the multiprincipal-element alloy mediate phonon and electron scattering.
Full phonon dispersion and scattering information provide a more complete description of temperature-dependent lattice transport.
Independent treatment of phonon and electronic contributions permits more precise agreement with experimental conductivity data.
Earlier approaches combine or approximate heat-carrier contributions and fail to capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity.
The proposed method will reduce predictive error by roughly 50% relative to earlier approaches.
Below 200 K, the predictions will agree with measurements that resolve comparable lattice and electronic contributions.
From 300 to 1200 K, the model will predict total conductivity within 10–17 W/(K·m).
The proposed applicability is restricted to defect-free bulk HfNbTaTiZr and the stated low- and high-temperature intervals.
Controlled isotope scattering can help isolate the lattice thermal-conductivity contribution.
Magnetic-field-sensitive measurements can help isolate the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution.
An error exceeding 15% for either isolated contribution, or failure to predict high-temperature total conductivity within 10–17 W/(K·m), falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The system is repeatedly restricted to a perfect, defect-free bulk crystal, but the high-temperature target explicitly contains 1 wt.% oxygen. An oxygen-bearing alloy is not the same ideal defect-free material unless oxygen is explicitly incorporated as a modeled substitutional or interstitial species and the meaning of 'defect-free' is narrowed to exclude only vacancies, dislocations, and microstructural defects.
